{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-nj-d","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"9ffcdcd512028b01ec563a6932b2597c5961afca523a483b0c8de4e755b20e57","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-nj-class-d:lineage:32","source_registry_sha256":"057b72c7c679c997f56ae00ef97a6b14dbe264551f4121b9bf67b0457d9cf7c1","source_liveness_sha256":"1ca7bfbb9e3c0a6b19e5e808ecab6fe8329f3b4799e394abc260d65c1d6513e7"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Defensive driving: crash prevention, distraction, fatigue, following distance, passing and bad-weather control","heading":"C — Defensive driving: the crash-prevention formula, aggressive driving and road rage, distractions, drowsy driving, communicating, following distances, lane changes and passing, wet roads and hydroplaning, snow and ice, and reduced visibility","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Defensive driving: the crash-prevention formula, aggressive driving and road rage, distractions, drowsy driving, communicating, following distances, lane changes and passing, wet roads and hydroplaning, snow and ice, and reduced visibility
Knowledge domain: the habits that keep a New Jersey driver out of crashes — staying alert and calm, recognizing aggressive driving, avoiding distraction and fatigue, signaling intentions, keeping enough following distance, changing lanes and passing safely, and controlling the vehicle on wet, snowy, icy, foggy or glare-filled roads.

FACT_ID: sec08-F01 | anchor: A01
Most crashes are caused by driver error. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec08-F02 | anchor: A01
The standard crash-prevention formula is to be alert, be prepared and act in time: never assume other drivers will not make mistakes, expect the unexpected, and avoid panic. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec08-F03 | anchor: A01
Aggressive driving is a progression of unlawful acts such as sudden changes of speed, improper or erratic lane changes, ignoring traffic control devices, failing to yield and following too closely. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0092]

FACT_ID: sec08-F04 | anchor: A02
To report an aggressive driver, call (888) SAF-ROAD, or #77 from a cell phone. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec08-F05 | anchor: A02
Even though the handheld phone law has emergency exceptions, the safest choice is to stop at the roadside first and only then place a call. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0093]

FACT_ID: sec08-F06 | anchor: A03
The four types of driving distraction are visual (eyes off the road), manual (hands off the wheel), cognitive (mind off driving) and auditory (sounds that pull attention away). [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec08-F07 | anchor: A03
Distractions are one of the leading causes of crashes for teen drivers, and a few seconds of inattention at highway speed can cover the length of a football field. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec08-F08 | anchor: A03
Common distractions include texting, scrolling or watching videos, using a phone even hands-free, programming a GPS while moving, picking music, taking photos, eating or drinking, turning to talk to passengers, reaching for items and using smart watches. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec08-F09 | anchor: A03
A tired driver reacts more slowly, gets upset more easily, may fall asleep at the wheel, and can be as dangerous as a drunk driver. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec08-F10 | anchor: A03
Maggie's Law, enacted in June 2003, makes it illegal to knowingly drive while impaired by lack of sleep and treats fatigued driving as recklessness under the vehicular homicide statute. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec08-F11 | anchor: A03
Highway hypnosis is a trance-like state after long periods at the wheel, and it can be avoided by never fixing your eyes on one thing for more than a few seconds. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0094]

FACT_ID: sec08-F12 | anchor: A04
On long drives, rest every two hours or share the driving with another licensed driver. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec08-F13 | anchor: A04
Those most at risk of drowsy driving include sleep-deprived people, drivers on long trips without breaks or driving when they would normally sleep, people on sleep-inducing medicine or alcohol, solo drivers, drivers on long rural roads, young people, shift workers and commercial drivers. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec08-F14 | anchor: A04
Communicate with other drivers by turn or hand signals, eye contact, a tap of the horn when needed, and at night a quick switch from low beams to high and back. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0095]

FACT_ID: sec08-F15 | anchor: A05
Tailgating means following the vehicle ahead too closely; it is a common cause of crashes and can set off a chain of rear-end collisions. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0096]

FACT_ID: sec08-F16 | anchor: A05
The usual rule of thumb is to stay one car length, about 20 feet, back for every 10 mph of speed, and to leave more room at high speed or in bad weather. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0096]

FACT_ID: sec08-F17 | anchor: A06
Under the three-seconds-plus rule, pick a fixed object ahead, start counting when the vehicle in front passes it, and you have enough room for a sudden stop if you need at least three seconds to reach it. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec08-F18 | anchor: A06
In bad weather, lengthen the following interval to four seconds or more. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec08-F19 | anchor: A06
The manual defines stopping distance as perception distance plus reaction distance plus braking distance. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec08-F20 | anchor: A06
Keeping a foot close to the brake reduces reaction distance, and heavier vehicles may take longer to stop. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0097]

FACT_ID: sec08-F21 | anchor: A07
The manual's minimum following distance table for ideal roads is 2 car lengths at 20 mph, 3 at 30 mph, 4 at 40 mph and 5 at 50 mph. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0098]

FACT_ID: sec08-F22 | anchor: A07
On wet pavement the table doubles those figures to 4 car lengths at 20 mph, 6 at 30 mph, 8 at 40 mph and 10 at 50 mph. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0098]

FACT_ID: sec08-F23 | anchor: A07
When changing lanes, never straddle a lane: check the rearview mirror, glance back at the blind spot and always signal. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0098]

FACT_ID: sec08-F24 | anchor: A07
After passing, signal and return to the right lane only when well ahead of the passed vehicle, a good sign being that you can see it in your rearview mirror, then cancel the signal. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0098]

FACT_ID: sec08-F25 | anchor: A08
When another vehicle passes you, stay in your lane and slow down to make the pass easier, then resume normal speed once it is well ahead. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0099]

FACT_ID: sec08-F26 | anchor: A08
On wet roads, drive more slowly, stop and turn with great care, and avoid quick turns or speed changes that can start a skid. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0099]

FACT_ID: sec08-F27 | anchor: A08
Tires can begin to hydroplane, riding on a film of water, at about 35 mph, and the risk grows as speed increases. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0099]

FACT_ID: sec08-F28 | anchor: A08
Above 55 mph tires may lose contact with the road entirely, and then braking becomes virtually impossible and turning impossible. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0099]

FACT_ID: sec08-F29 | anchor: A08
To avoid hydroplaning, do not drive on bald or badly worn tires, slow down in heavy rain, standing water or slush, and in a downpour use the highest part of the road, such as the center lane. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0099]

FACT_ID: sec08-F30 | anchor: A09
In cold weather, warm up the engine as the manufacturer directs and remove all snow and ice from the entire vehicle before driving. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0100]

FACT_ID: sec08-F31 | anchor: A09
New Jersey law holds a driver responsible for ice that flies off the vehicle and causes death, injury or property damage. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0100]

FACT_ID: sec08-F32 | anchor: A09
A vehicle skids when the driver accelerates too quickly, turns too fast or brakes improperly. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0100]

FACT_ID: sec08-F33 | anchor: A10
On snow and ice, drivers with ABS keep a foot on the brake pedal without pumping, while conventional disc and drum brakes need firm, steady pressure. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0101]

FACT_ID: sec08-F34 | anchor: A10
If conventional brakes lock, release the pedal and reapply at once with slightly less pressure, repeating with less and less pressure until the vehicle is under control. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0101]

FACT_ID: sec08-F35 | anchor: A10
Snow tires give better traction in winter but not on ice, and tire chains give the best traction on ice and in hard-packed or deep snow. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0101]

FACT_ID: sec08-F36 | anchor: A10
In New Jersey, studded snow tires may be used between November 15 and April 1. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0101]

FACT_ID: sec08-F37 | anchor: A10
To start on snow or ice, keep the engine speed low, shift to a lower gear if the wheels spin, and rock between forward and reverse if stuck. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0101]

FACT_ID: sec08-F38 | anchor: A10
On snow-covered roads, a good rule is a following distance of six seconds or more. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0101]

FACT_ID: sec08-F39 | anchor: A10
In fog, always slow down, keep the headlights on low beam and switch on fog lights if the vehicle has them. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0101]

FACT_ID: sec08-F40 | anchor: A10
Whenever visibility is greatly reduced, pull off alongside the road or onto the shoulder, out of traffic, and turn on the emergency flashers. [A10]
Source: [A10 -> pdf-0101]

Misconceptions: driving slower than traffic is not automatically safer, keeping up with the flow is part of safe driving; a hands-free call is still a distraction; snow tires do not grip ice, chains do; high beams in fog are wrong, use low beams; drowsy driving can be a crime under Maggie's Law, not just a bad habit.
Mnemonics: three seconds in good weather, four or more in bad weather, six or more on snow; hydroplaning starts around thirty-five and above fifty-five the tires can lift off completely; one car length for every ten miles per hour; studded tires from mid-November to the first of April.
Glossary: aggressive driving means a chain of unlawful moves such as erratic lane changes and tailgating; road rage means aggressive driving that boils over into anger at others; highway hypnosis means a trance-like state on long drives; hydroplaning means tires riding up on a film of water; tailgating means following too closely; three-seconds-plus rule means the counting method for judging following distance.
Dynamic facts: the aggressive-driver hotline numbers and the studded tire season can change; confirm them on official New Jersey websites.
